Oral evidence - 18 Nov 2026

Health and Social Care Committee

Oral evidence: Health and Homelessness, HC 750

Wednesday 17 November 2026

Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 17 November 2026.

Watch the meeting

Members present: Layla Moran (Chair); Sadik Al-Hassan; Danny Beales; Ben Coleman; Andrew George.

Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee member present: Andrew Cooper.

Questions 1 - 141

Witnesses

I: Alex Bax, Chief Executive, Pathway; Peter Moore, Programme Manager, Oxfordshire Health and Homelessness Inclusion Team, Oxford City Council; Edward Redshaw, Homeless Health Lead and Consultant, Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust.

II: Alison McGovern MP, Minister for Social Care and Mental Health, Department of Health and Social Care; Natasha Burgon, Director of Health Improvement, Department of Health and Social Care; Catherine Bennion, Director, Homelessness and Rough Sleeping, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; Lesley Watts, Regional Director for London, NHS England.

Examination of witnesses

Witnesses: Alex Bax, Peter Moore and Edward Redshaw.

Chair: Welcome to this one-off session of the Health and Social Care Committee where we will be looking at health and homelessness. We have two panels today. Would the first panel mind introducing yourselves, please, and what you do?

Peter Moore: I am Peter Moore. I am the programme manager for the Oxfordshire health and homelessness inclusion team.

Alex Bax: Good morning, everyone. I am Alex Bax. I am chief executive of Pathway, the national homeless and inclusion health charity.

Edward Redshaw: I am Edward Redshaw. I am the clinical lead for the homeless health team at Imperial NHS trust.

Chair: Thank you very much. In the first panel, we want to discuss a little bit of the wider picture. I just wanted to kick us off by asking a few questions about data. I was really struck and quite alarmed to find that there is no fixed way of measuring in hospitals whether someone is homeless: 31 trusts use address records such as no fixed abode, but six trusts say homelessness is not routinely recorded at all. Alex, what is going on?

Alex Bax: You are right. What you have found is absolutely true. There is no consistent approach across the NHS to recording people’s housing status. That is the fundamental problem.

Chair: Why not?

Alex Bax: There is a lack of impetus. We have done a lot of work over the years to create a set of standardised housing status fields. We have had them adopted in the emergency care dataset and the NHS urgent care dataset. They are available. They are things like “rough sleeper”, “sofa surfer”, and so on. They are a set of agreed typologies that we have tested with some lived experience colleagues as well.

They are in the background, but they are not highlighted to frontline staff. They are not trained on them, so people do not use them. When you ask someone to review the data against those fields, it is often absent—the box is not ticked. It is not mandatory. One question would be whether it should be made it a mandatory step when you are clerking a patient. It feels like inertia—that it is never quite a priority for anybody to make this happen.

There is a parallel issue that sometimes asking about someone’s housing status is a non-trivial question. With homelessness, we know there is a certain degree of shame sometimes, so people may feel uncomfortable, say, in A&E.

Chair: Is that on the part of the clinician generally?

Alex Bax: On the clinician’s part there is a question of, “Oh my goodness, I might be opening a can of worms. What am I going to do if I discover something bad? Who am I going to call? Perhaps I will not ask.”

From the patient perspective, being asked about my housing status in public, when it may be insecure or when I do not know what is going to happen, may again cause me to feel nervous, particularly if I am in a public space.

Chair: What is the best guess at the moment for discharge to homelessness numbers? The range is quite extraordinary: there are numbers from 100 a month from the Government to 10,000 a year. Even if you times 100 a month by 12, you still do not get anywhere near that—it is a factor of 10 difference. Do we have a central estimate?

Alex Bax: In a true sense, we do not know. We do not have good data on it. I think you are referring to the Salvation Army, which has done an FOI recently that found 10,000 discharges to the street. Of course, discharged to the street is the most extreme example. Many patients would be discharged into other forms of homelessness, such as chronically insecure or inappropriate accommodation that is highly likely to break down. That 10,000 number is plainly an underestimate. Bluntly, we do not know.

Chair: Peter, the data that we can see suggests that the number of rough sleepers who have recently left hospital is relatively stable. Does that match what you are actually seeing on the ground?

Peter Moore: I can only speak for Oxford and Oxfordshire really. What I have seen, certainly in the last five years since the out-of-hospital programme, is a great reduction in discharge to rough sleeping but, as Alex was saying, discharge to all types of homelessness and the homelessness duties that local authorities are picking up are reasonably stable. There has been a big impact on the actual discharge to street, I would suggest; I have seen it.

Chair: What are the particular pressures that you are seeing in Oxford? How is that changing over time?

Peter Moore: It is the same pressure that is always there around a lack of affordable housing; that is the overarching pressure in Oxfordshire. There are a multitude of pressures, but one would be that the system is not quite set up to be a seven-day service. In the out-of-hospital team, as it was then, and now the OHHI team, we trialled having weekend embedded housing and trying to support weekend discharges, but it would need a system-wide approach to that, which may come through recent neighbourhood developments and more integrated ways of thinking. Cost of living is another pressure.

Chair: When you say recent neighbourhood developments, which ones are you pinning your hopes on?

Peter Moore: We are seeing a lot more genuine movement around integrating our services in Oxfordshire. We have really good partnership working and have had for a number of years now, whether that is through commissioning or how we actually operate.

Chair: Who is driving that?

Peter Moore: The city council has been strong in that, because it commissioned the OHHI model, but it has had great support from the county, Oxford Health, OUH and partners there. There is really genuine and strong partnership support in that.

What are we pinning our hopes on? The neighbourhood services that are being rolled out and neighbourhood planning. The city council and housing have been involved in that from quite an early stage and continue to be. I can talk more about that if you want, but I do not want to take up too much time. On that and the rough sleeping programme, we are seeing some concrete actions coming out of that.

Chair: Edward, on data, do you have any views about how we help to smooth this out? How do we get a correct picture about what is actually going on out there? If we cannot measure it, we cannot mend it, can we?

Edward Redshaw: The model that we have introduced at Imperial is that homelessness is coded as a diagnosis problem. On A&E and discharge summaries, it is one of the diagnoses that is there, which then follows through into the GP record as well. That is the plan.

Obviously, the implementation of that requires buy-in from the people who write those summaries and the junior doctors on the wards who rotate very frequently. It is a continual, educational process in the hospital to make sure that that goal is maintained.

That is probably the best way, because often things are put in free text that then are not coded and do not come under the data. If you code it as an actual problem, that will then be showing up in the data as well. That is our model that we use at the moment.

Alex Bax: That shows the value of the specialist homeless team in a hospital. Most hospitals in this country do not have those kinds of teams, which are the teams Pathway helps to support. Without that team, there is nobody to do that work. There is nobody to go to the junior doctor rotation round to do the teaching again and again, so you get a flurry of activity because there is a bit of an initiative, and then it decays, and six months later people are not doing it again.

It is one of those exercises where you need to introduce it and then keep it operational. Without a focus within the hospital—and we would say, without a team focused on this patient group—it just decays endlessly.

Andrew George: Following the information you just provided, to what extent are the post-discharge circumstances of patients tracked? Is there any monitoring? In other words, in the weeks or months after discharge, for those who were experiencing rough sleeping, do we know whether the hospital episode might have helped to correct the rough sleeping lifestyle that patients experienced beforehand?

Edward Redshaw: In our data, we record the circumstances of people’s housing situations at admission and at discharge for all the patients who come under our team. We will not have the long-term follow-up in our data.

Peter Moore: For people who access the OHHI services, with their consent we record a reasonable amount of data. We have had to do that to make the case for ongoing funding. Some of that increasingly becomes about longer-term outcomes, and we have seen the impact.

We are lucky to have quite a good provision of step services, so rehab or respite out of hospital, and also preventive community admissions. We are able to now see some of the impact of those services on people’s readmission rates, presentation to emergency departments and ongoing housing outcomes. There is quite a big impact on all of that.

Alex Bax: The metrics Ed mentioned are the metrics we encourage all teams to operate on from admission to discharge in order to track change in housing status. The follow-up question is really hard. Oxfordshire are leading the way to some extent. Without proper connections between the hospital and the community, you are just not following the patients, and that includes in data.

London hospitals are particularly challenging because the patients at Imperial will come from all over the place and they will go back all over the place, so that is tricky. The NHS knows who we all are in theory, so it should be possible from a health perspective to follow it up.

Andrew George: One would have thought so. There has been no effort to undertake a proactive research study to monitor the point at which that person is six months after discharge, for example.

Alex Bax: There have been some studies. Our own randomised controlled trial of the Pathway hospital team followed patients up for six months and found that patients who were attended by the hospital staff plus a Pathway team were in a much better housing circumstance six months post discharge than the patients who just got standard care. We know this hospital team intervention very significantly affects people’s housing status at the six-month point.

The negative finding, which was really interesting, was that many of the patients in the non-intervention arm of that study were untraceable, could not be found or were in such terrible circumstances that the students we had following them up asked to stop doing it because it was too distressing for the students. It is possible to follow up the positive outcomes, but there is this other group, if you are not doing anything, who just disappear back into the morass of homelessness.

Andrew George: It would be useful to have that. If there is material on that, it would be enormously helpful to have an indication as to the proportions and how that works if intelligence is available.

Can you just talk us through the discharge pathway, or rather the pathway of the patient once they are admitted to the hospital? What happens? What is the process they go through? How do you capture the information that you have referred to already, and what about at the point of discharge and the management of that?

Edward Redshaw: Our team in the hospital relies on the ward teams in hospital to identify homelessness. The clinicians are admitting the patient into the hospital, and then there are also the discharge teams who are the teams in the wards who start to think about what will happen after the patient leaves. They highlight all the people with either unstable housing or nowhere safe to go to, or the people who were rough sleeping on admission.

We receive a referral from those teams, ideally as soon as possible. That is one of the metrics that we try to really promote. We need to be referred the patient as soon as possible on admission, because the work starts right at the beginning of the admission.

Andrew George: Is that to the local authority housing officers?

Edward Redshaw: First of all, it is to our in-patient team, and that is then where we complete a comprehensive assessment of the patient, detail all the needs, their situation and their previous housing history, and start to look at the barriers that have caused them to be in this situation.

Often, the next step is a duty to refer sent to their local authority, which starts the homelessness application with their local authority. That process takes time. In our situation in London, it usually leads to some form of emergency accommodation being provided by the council. We do not really have access to any specific step-down accommodation, so we are making homelessness applications through that to the local council through the duty-to-refer process.

Andrew George: We are talking in the main about what are known as P1 pathways for discharge, because obviously in other circumstances there is simply a discharge to a community hospital or to a care home.

Chair: Can I just briefly bring in our colleague from the HCLG Committee, Andrew Cooper?

Andrew Cooper: I am interested in the point you make about the duty to refer, which came in in the Homelessness Reduction Act 2017. You were saying earlier that a hospital is not necessarily systematically recording whether someone is homeless when they are admitted. In your view, how can the hospital possibly be complying with the duty to refer if they are not recording that information?

Edward Redshaw: They are recording it as a code.

Andrew Cooper: Is it systematically recorded for every patient?

Edward Redshaw: We have worked with the A&E doctors. It is not systematic in that it is requested for every single patient. One of the key questions that a doctor will ask is the social situation of a patient, so it would certainly be expected that they would identify that in a medical assessment.

Andrew Cooper: Perhaps things are working particularly well in your hospital, but if that had been missed, would the hospital be complying with their duty to refer if they had not recorded the information in the first place? In your view, does the duty to refer encompass capturing the information in the first place?

Edward Redshaw: It would certainly be helpful, yes.

Alex Bax: We have done a lot of work on this. Again, teams such as Ed’s are exceptional. We have helped create 20 of them, but there are large numbers of hospitals where I would say that you are absolutely right: the hospitals do not do this routinely. It happens sometimes because some wards or some people will have paid attention to it, but it is not currently routine in the way lots of staff are trained, because they are busy and have loads of other stuff to do, and it just does not get the attention.

Andrew Cooper: Local authorities have a statutory duty to prevent homelessness, whereas in the NHS you just have the duty to refer. Do you think that the duty to prevent homelessness ought to be extended to encompass hospital trusts or ICBs?

Alex Bax: That is a tricky question because they do not have the power in terms of providing accommodation, which is fundamentally one of the problems of homelessness. It would be difficult to impose that on the NHS per se. We are interested in these duties to collaborate. For the NHS to be very present in this problem is absolutely right, and then it is about how you frame that. Putting a duty to prevent homelessness on a hospital would be tricky, because they would fail to meet their duty if the local authority was failing to meet its duty, if you see what I mean.

Chair: We grapple with these things all the time.

Peter Moore: You were talking about what we are hoping for and pinning our hopes on in Oxfordshire, and I was talking about partnership working. We are developing a suite of performance measures and KPIs that we hold ourselves accountable to through the prevention of homelessness directors group, and one of those is that hospitals and housing commit together to no discharge to street, and that is measured and they are held accountable to it. It is not a duty as such, but it is acting as if there is one. We are trialling that.

Alex Bax: We need really strong connections between health, housing and social care.

Andrew Cooper: My concern is that earlier on you mentioned that sometimes these services get put in place, and they are working quite well but then they tail off. It is just about how we make sure that they do not tail off and that they are embedded in the culture. I hope we can flesh that out a little bit.

Andrew George: Alex, you were saying that the situation with regard to the Imperial project, which Ed was responsible for, is exceptional. I do not know whether any of you have a national picture as to how exceptional that is, and how unexceptional—

Alex Bax: Pathway as a charity was founded around the creation of the first ever specialist homeless team in hospital at UCLH in 2009. We have helped to create 21 such teams since then around the country.

Andrew George: What proportion is that?

Alex Bax: That is perhaps 25%. We would say there are still 40 or 50 to go.

Andrew George: This is following a gold standard.

Alex Bax: Is it a gold standard? Dream on, but we are following a good standard. We could always think of more things.

Andrew George: It is a bronze standard, then.

Alex Bax: A good standard is having a Pathway team, and we know there are 20 or so. We have NICE guidance; we have all this evidence; we have randomised controlled trials. We therefore know there are large numbers of hospitals where this approach is not followed and where we do not know what is going on, but from other work we know, for example, that the duty to refer is not well followed in places where there is no focused team.

Andrew George: The national plan to end homelessness says the Government will work with the NHS and the council to implement existing guidance. What does the Department of Health need to do to ensure that the guidance is actually implemented? Is there anything more?

Alex Bax: The NICE guidance is very clear that two things—specialist teams in hospitals and intermediate care—would make a huge step towards dealing with this problem from the hospital perspective.

Telling the system to implement more guidance that has already been issued is not enough. It needs a more assertive approach of some sort to try to make this happen across the whole of the NHS as opposed to the places where we as a nice charity or great leaders drive it locally. Can we generalise this now?

Andrew George: Do you mean “assertive” in the sense of being promotional? It cannot come with a big stick or anything.

Alex Bax: Yes, or money. We observe significant new money from the Prime Minister coming into MHCLG, but we do not observe any additional funding coming into the Department of Health and Social Care.

I was at an OECD meeting on this theme last week. Observably, in 55% of OECD members, the problem of homelessness exists and the Department of State that has the lead is the welfare Department.

Andrew George: Did you say the OECD?

Alex Bax: The OECD is exploring homelessness internationally. In the majority of countries, the problem is owned by the health or welfare Department, not by the housing Department, which is interesting.

Peter Moore: To back up Alex’s point, it is about national leadership on this and using the evidence and the data about what we know works to roll it out across the nation. That is where we are at. We have good data now. We actually have good evidence of what is effective. We need to roll that out.

Andrew George: The Government have a target of ending rough sleeping and have published new guidance setting out the actions for the health and care sector in that regard. Does this provide the support, direction and push that you are describing?

Alex Bax: The push is extremely welcome, and the energy that has arrived with Andy Burnham is really noticeable in the funding. In health, it still feels like the guidance is being issued. The health service has a lot of guidance and there is no programmatic focus to say, “Shall we implement the guidance?” You need to support the system to implement the guidance, which may need money, leadership and so on to actually make it happen in systems.

To respond to Andrew’s point, it is then about having some kind of monitoring and accountability so that services do not decay one or two years in, so that it is now something we have in our system that is standard.

Andrew George: In relation to the 75% that are not meeting the good standard that you believe has been achieved in some locations, are you saying that patients who were rough sleeping prior to admission are being discharged on a P1 discharge system back to rough sleeping?

Alex Bax: That is very likely.

Andrew George: It is very likely in 75% of cases.

Alex Bax: It is worth saying that some of those hospitals probably have some great staff doing some great work that we are not aware of, but yes, it is very likely. In some of those hospitals, absolutely, people would be discharged to usual care—because it said on the notes they were homeless on the street before, that is usual care. There are all kinds of ways this is described.

Andrew George: You are also saying that, in many cases, the hospital will not even be aware of it. Possibly in most cases they will not be aware of it.

Alex Bax: Many staff across the NHS will be aware of it because they find it. It is not something staff want to do.

Andrew George: What challenge do you face in recruiting and retaining clinical and support staff to run care transfer hubs and other health services aimed at supporting those at risk of being discharged into homelessness? How does it compare with other specialist areas?

Alex Bax: We were talking about this beforehand. Systematically, the main problem for the services we support in our network is short-term funding. Again, it is not standardised, so it is funded by a pilot programme—a bit of end of year, a bit of this and a bit of that—which means you cannot sustain a team. We have a couple of teams on our network at the moment who have no budget agreed. From 31 March next year, they have no salary budget in prospect, so staff are beginning to look for other jobs.

Andrew George: Are they third-sector employees?

Alex Bax: No, these are NHS.

Andrew George: They are all NHS. When you say “short-term”, how short?

Alex Bax: The funding is sometimes a year; sometimes it is less than that, but the colleagues here are both in the fabulous position of having longer-term budgets, which have allowed them to create teams and services that are sustained.

Chair: Peter was disputing that with his hands.

Peter Moore: I am very appreciative of the funding we get. We are well supported, principally by the better care fund, with some rough sleeping initiative money, but it is still month to month. Everything that Alex is saying about recruitment and retention, but also development, developing your team and what we are talking about regarding losing knowledge, skills and momentum, is not helped by that short-term funding.

Also, if you are looking at step services and intermediate care, it makes it very hard to acquire and strategically plan for acquiring suitable properties. You end up having to do what you can.

Chair: Yes, we are going to come to that specifically in a moment.

Edward Redshaw: We saw the impact of the short-term funding on our team. We were very fortunate to have our funding extended to 2029 at the end of March this year, but we lost two of our workers during that period before that was confirmed, because of uncertainties and needing to leave. We have only just now rebuilt our team to be fully staffed because of that concern.

Alex Bax: The NICE guidance, which we think is very good—this is interesting for NICE guidance—made a point of saying to the system, “Please can we see minimum-term five-year contracts for services in this space”, because patients need that. Trusting relationships are at the heart of good homeless care. If you have short-term staff rolling over, you do not get that. It is also about building the knowledge base; the way the teams work and embed themselves into local services takes time.

Chair: Just to be clear, if that had happened, you could have been more efficient with the same money. Is that what I am hearing?

Peter Moore: Yes, absolutely. Recruitment costs money; retraining costs money. If you are a higher-performing team, then yes, you would deliver more and you would be more efficient.

Andrew George: Who actually makes that decision? Is it the ICB or is it further up the food chain?

Peter Moore: Some 98% of our funding comes through the better care fund, and it works on a year-to-year package. As I understand it, the funding decisions are made in a collaborative, partnership way with the better care fund planning group, which is fantastic, but the actual funding package coming down the line comes centrally.

Andrew George: You are uncertain of where those decisions are made about the length of funding invested.

Peter Moore: I am.

Andrew George: Okay, and none of the rest of you knows.

Edward Redshaw: It is the ICB.

Andrew George: It is the ICB in your case.

Alex Bax: We have a team at St George’s in south London, for example, where two roles are funded by City Hall, one is funded by the council, one is funded by the trust and one is funded by the ICB. Again, from a management point of view, you can see that this is not a stable way to run a service.

Andrew George: Those at risk of homelessness or experiencing homelessness often require support, of course, from multiple services. It is not entirely down to the NHS to resolve their problems, but in the process of discharging, clearly you need to be working with others in that process. Are there significant barriers to effective joint working between your services and local authorities, for example?

Edward Redshaw: One of the challenges is what Alex mentioned. We have patients at Imperial from many London boroughs. We have good connections with the boroughs that are most local to the hospital, but to further forge the relationships for patients in the outer London boroughs is difficult. We do not always get as good responses or buy-in to the MDT meetings that we have because we just do not have those same connections with outer London.

Andrew George: Then there are practical considerations such as, inevitably, discharge at weekends or out-of-office hours. You are all nodding, so that is an issue. In terms of out-of-hours contact with other agencies, there are limitations as to what is available.

Edward Redshaw: We are quite supported by the clinicians, and the outcome of the lack of weekend services from our team is that people stay in hospital over the weekend, so you have the pressure on the hospital increased for discharges. That is the clear impact of that.

Alex Bax: There is a real grinding of the cogs here. Hospitals are 24 hours a day, seven days a week services. Nobody else is.

Andrew George: A lot of them have out-of-hours emergency contact numbers for emergency homelessness and emergency need.

Peter Moore: Absolutely, they all do. Local authorities will do. If my health colleagues were here, they would say that that can be inconsistent, depending on the situation.

Andrew George: Is it inconsistent from borough to borough or from local authority to local authority, or within the authority itself?

Peter Moore: All of the above. It can be very good, but it can be exceptionally time-consuming for somebody at 2 am in an emergency department to try to co-ordinate that and to be waiting for a call back or trying to get through. Sometimes it can go very smoothly. That whole 24/7 service would be something that I would really like to see looked at.

Alex Bax: A very significant further barrier is the barrier of the administrative lock around the patient’s complex situation, which is key. Our team is particularly at the moment reporting problems with adult social care, which is unsurprising.

For many of our patients, with assessment and the kind of work Ed does, you can see that they would be entitled to some social care. You sometimes cannot get the social care package until you have determined which local authority owes them a housing duty, because they may have been moving around, so you are into these endless bureaucratic cycles between housing departments and social care departments, getting people over thresholds, which falls on the hospital team.

Chair: It is hard enough when you are clear where they belong.

Alex Bax: Yes. That social care impediment is very significant.

Peter Moore: Just on that point, we are lucky enough to have social workers in our team. I agree with Alex. If we did not have that, I imagine it would be much harder, but to have them in as part of the MDT is really powerful.

Andrew George: The national plan has a duty to collaborate. Do you think that will actually help any of those issues? Do you have any indication as to whether that is going to change cultures?

Alex Bax: It is in the implementation. What does it mean in reality? Again, our model is of a mixed MDT. You have clinical staff, social work qualified staff, housing staff and lived experience in the same team. That gives you a good chance of navigating all these different systems for the patient, but you also need the bureaucracies behind to be collaborative and supporting each other.

Andrew George: Pathway has raised the particular challenges that are faced when discharging a patient who has no recourse to public funds. What is the proposed solution to that, particularly as the Government are under a lot of political pressure, from the right at least, to cut the welfare budget?

Alex Bax: It is very tricky. For 20% of the homeless patients seen by our teams in London hospitals, it is considered on their first review that they might have no recourse. Very often it is not clear, and indeed when you then engage with the patient and staff, many of that group do actually have recourse when you look at their circumstances. You can make many of them into people who have rights.

Andrew George: Is that because they are not getting the advice about their entitlements?

Alex Bax: Yes, they have not had advice or they believe they will be refused, so they have stayed away.

Andrew George: One area of assistance while they are captured within the hospital is to give them welfare rights advice.

Alex Bax: We have spent quite a lot of time over the years proving the benefit of trying, again, to get access to specialist immigration and legal advice for teams such as Ed’s. We have funded it charitably sometimes. We have just got the east London ICB to fund it for the teams in east London. It helps. Where there are eastern Europeans who have “failed to exercise their treaty rights”, because they did not know they had to exercise their treaty rights and then they have got sick, if you can get some immigration advice around them, you can get a yes or no. If they are definitely “no recourse”, it is helpful to be clear. Where they have recourse and you can establish it, that is also extremely helpful.

Again, the hospital episode could be, philosophically, a great point of clarification for our patients in all kinds of ways. This is another area where you can make quite a difference if you can set up access to legal advice.

Andrew George: This is another area of collaboration and co-ordination of services. Thank you.

Andrew Cooper: We started to touch on intermediary care, which, as you all know, allows people to recover after hospital and tries to reduce discharge to the street. How much intermediary care space for people experiencing or at risk of homelessness is needed to meet demand in your areas?

Peter Moore: We are very lucky to have 36 beds in Oxfordshire, a majority in Oxford city but some in the north of the county. That is not far off the number we need. To be fair, there are people we cannot support through that, but that is partly down to the issue we were talking about with short-term funding, so the suitability of properties for people’s needs—for example, mobility needs. We are also increasingly getting referrals for people who are much older, with quite high support needs around medication and who are experiencing homelessness.

With the right backing to refine the model, we would not need much more than we currently have. Maybe we need more disbursement around the county and more specialists; step-plus is what I would say.

Edward Redshaw: We have virtually none for the Imperial team. Even a small unit would make a big difference. The Royal London and the Homerton hospitals have small, six-bed services, which is a significant addition to their service.

For the most complex cases where we do not have any other suitable options through the pathways we talked about before, that is where it would allow a huge level of follow-up and impact. We are not talking about huge units, but a six or 12-bed unit would be fantastic for our team and would make a massive difference.

Andrew Cooper: I am interested in what you have in place in Oxfordshire. Obviously, someone who has experienced homelessness will generally have quite a lot of trauma that has gone along with that. There may be mental health issues or addiction issues that are going alongside that. Is the intermediary care that you have set up to deal with that? Do you work in partnership with your local mental health trust?

Peter Moore: Absolutely, it is set up. It is delivered by PCSE partners who are commissioned through the model, with two of them to deliver the service. They are very skilled and take a very relational approach to working with patients or clients through overt intervention, so it is slightly longer-term although it is a short stay. They can move on with support from the same organisations in their journey.

While in step-down, they have access to in-reach from our own clinical OHHI team. We have social workers, psychologists, a mental health practitioner, OTs and a physical health nurse. It is that wrap-around support that people are talking about.

Actually addressing the effects of lifetime embedded trauma is one of the biggest impacts that our team can have, working slightly outside of the statutory mainstream, although, of course, highly linked to it. That approach is invaluable.

As I am sure colleagues at the table will attest, we have had people with the most traumatic stories and the hardest lives, maybe spending 40 years in a tent on a roundabout. That stay in step-down is the first time that they have caught their breath, in a way, and that someone has been able to ask them, “What do you want? What do you need?”, and co-create that plan together.

Although there will be many other factors, some of those other factors are put into place while in step-down, and it is that MDT planning and working directly with the clients, so it is not done to them, that is extremely powerful. You were talking about readmission rates and longer-term outcomes; we have strong data to back that up.

Andrew Cooper: Alex, can you paint us a picture of what it looks like on the national scene?

Alex Bax: Again, it is in the NICE guidance. We know that having the team in the hospital plus intermediate care gets very much better outcomes for this patient group. It very substantially interrupts homelessness and returns people to life, if you like.

The challenge in London, if I may, just before you come in and clarify this, is that virtually every local authority is facing major issues when it comes to supporting people who have homeless needs. It is expensive and is out of proportion with all of London, but the cuts that London councils—not just four or five, but over a dozen or perhaps even more—are having to make as a result of the reduction in Government funding for London are going to exacerbate the problem for local authorities.

All the guidance that you issue and all the pressure that you are trying to apply through the better care fund are going to be undermined by the huge fair funding cuts that London is going to experience.

Catherine Bennion: I can talk to the homelessness and rough sleeping funding, which is the formula on which we base that, and we do take into account homelessness and rough sleeping pressures. London has received a much bigger proportion of the recent funding on rough sleeping, which also took into account housing costs, than other places in the country. That funding is ringfenced for the purposes of homelessness.

Ben Coleman: How much more has it received?

Catherine Bennion: I will have to write and confirm, but I think it was about 95%.

Ben Coleman: What is it in pounds, shillings and pence?

Catherine Bennion: It is £168 million.

Ben Coleman: Most councils have received cuts of tens or twenties of millions of pounds. These are huge cuts. It is really a drop in the ocean against the overall cuts, is it not?

Catherine Bennion: That is just the rough sleeping programme.

Alison McGovern: As you know, Mr Coleman, I am very happy to talk about the fair funding review. In the end, dealing with this issue requires collaboration between health and local authorities, and for us to get better quality temporary accommodation that also has the added benefit of costing councils less.

Chair: You mentioned that the review of the guidance for the better care fund is still ongoing, but that you are soon going to be releasing new guidance particularly about this. Is this different guidance? I am just trying to get a sense of the timelines here. Minister, you are saying that there is a review happening soon.

Natasha Burgon: I might have said the wrong words. It is the 2027-28 better care fund framework, which is due to be published shortly.

Chair: So the guidance that you are talking about, Minister, will come out sooner than that review is completed. Is that correct?

Natasha Burgon: That framework will include guidance on things such as intermediate care, as we have been discussing.

Chair: You are not going to wait.

Alison McGovern: No, we have to publish—I am sorry if “guidance” was the wrong word—the framework for the fund every year.

Chair: In that will be the updated guidance on the homelessness bit of the better care fund that you cannot talk about at the moment, if it were included.

Alison McGovern: I cannot talk about it, but we are seized of the importance of this issue.

Chair: I want to move on to collaboration. I just want to understand, so that I am very clear, this duty to collaborate. From an MHCLG and a local authority perspective, what concretely will be different from the current duty to refer?

Catherine Bennion: The duty to refer is literally that. It just requires a notification of people who are—

Chair: You made the point earlier that it comes too late, at a point of crisis.

Catherine Bennion: It comes too late. The duty to collaborate will focus on prevention alongside supporting people who have become homeless or who are at risk of homelessness. Our hope is—and this has been implemented elsewhere—that that will make sure that there is more collaboration earlier to focus on prevention as well as the support that people might need when they enter crisis.

Chair: What concretely will look different? You have described what it is. What are you hoping will look different?

Catherine Bennion: I am hoping that all the agencies that will be covered by the duty, which we are due to specify in secondary legislation, will work together to prevent homelessness.

Chair: You are telling me again what it is. What will they have to do differently to do that, which they do not already do and that you do not have the powers to do?

Catherine Bennion: They will have to work together.

Alison McGovern: I might just interject. In the case that Mr Beales raised earlier, we have a worked example of a lack of collaboration. Lesley has talked about having strong multidisciplinary teams and real housing expertise as part of discharge. It is those kinds of collaborations that can make a difference, particularly because we are talking about people who, as Mr Al-Hassan mentioned, will often have a range of needs, so we might need to have mental health expertise there as well.

If the duty to collaborate comes into force and is legislated for, and once we have all of the approaches, what I want to see is easy co-ordination between housing options teams, mental health teams and NHS colleagues, so that people are both safe and supported into better housing, and not stuck in hospital because of a lack of housing option.

Chair: Just to be clear, they could already do that now. In fact, some places do. Is that right?

Alison McGovern: Some places do, but the question is about how we get the right institutional framework to make it much more likely and much closer to certain that it will happen.

Chair: So they could do it now, but they do not. You are hoping that legislating will mean that you will be able to hold them to account more easily, but there is an accountability framework that is currently being drafted anyway. What is the point of this?

Natasha Burgon: We are not waiting for the statutory duty. We are trying to also use the levers that we already have, by making it clear, in terms of leadership, what we are looking for on accountability and joint governance. A legislative lever helps in that. The guidance that will be published in November is all about having a holistic approach and joining up, having much more team around the person, and being trauma-informed, as your colleagues mentioned. An additional statutory duty gives us additional emphasis there. As Catherine mentioned, the secondary legislation, where we really specify the different organisations that we want involved, will help force a more joined-up approach.

Chair: Thank you, I think. We have had a number of occasions when we have legislated for particularly NHS-related things, and what ends up happening, especially with the turmoil in the system, is that the system is then incentivised to wait because it just does not know whose job is going to be where, let alone what the geographical areas will be and so on. Is there a risk, by having said that you are going to legislate, that you are in effect stopping people from actively wanting to engage with this? I am hearing no, but I am not convinced. Lesley, why do you shake your head?

Lesley Watts: The health service does want to actively engage in this and, indeed, on many occasions, does. One of the things that the Minister has asked me, and that I absolutely will do, is, at the next chief execs meeting, to go through the updated guidance and reiterate that. That is something that we have had a discussion on at the NHS executive, and we will talk about our commitment to doing this.

Chair: I am sorry, Minister, but just for the cleanliness of my mind, I need to better understand your reticence about the target point—just so that, when you write to me, we are both clear what it is that you are going to write to me about, and we are clear that we are getting the answer that we need. Help me here.

The guidance in section 3.4.2 says that no one eligible for homelessness services will be discharged to the street, so there already is a target. The target, in effect, is zero. Then we ask the question, “By when?” If you have the amorphous target of, “We want to achieve motherhood and apple pie at some point in the future,” but you do not say by when, our concern is—and I think we were all agreed—that, if you do not have something with a bit of bite, the system tends to try to ignore it. We had that conversation earlier.

What I am struggling to understand is, first of all, whether you are questioning this target. At points, it sounded like you might have been. You were worried that, if we have a target of no one, that would lead to perverse incentives in the systems where most vulnerable people are discharged. We had a conversation around that. Just for clarity, you agree that this is the target, that it is the right target, and that it is a target that we need to be achieving. Can I just clear that up?

Alison McGovern: Yes, I absolutely agree with that.

Chair: Therefore, what is the issue with setting a timebound target and then, arguably, interim targets within that?

Alison McGovern: We did get into a slight bit of confusion, because there is no discharge to the street, which is what we set in the plan, and that is our goal. Also, overall, we want to reduce the number of people who have no criteria to reside. That might lead you to think that we want nobody waiting for discharge because of homelessness, which is a slightly different thing.

If I may suggest a way forward on this, my point was that the goal is really clear in the plan. We just need to work through these issues about duty to collaborate, having the right pathways, having the right accountability and the data question about what the baseline is. We need to figure out what our path is. What you are saying, which is very clear, is, “Why not just make that public?” That is a question for us that is not unreasonable, and I will happily write to you with a response, having digested it.

Chair: At some stage, you will be able to write to us with a date by which you hope to achieve at least an interim target towards that zero. In prisons, for example, you have a 50% reduction target by the end of the Parliament. That is what we are looking for. At some point, are you going to be able to tell us that it will be, say, a 25% reduction by X time? Is that what we are aiming for?

Alison McGovern: I will write to you with a response on that, because it is the right thing to do to consider what our pathway is and to judge what the right thing would be, given all of the system complexities that we have. The goal is very clear in the plan. The Department of Health signed up to this plan when we published it. As you will have heard from colleagues, people within the NHS are very committed to it. Let me come back to you with what the right way would be to approach a public target on that.

Andrew Cooper: I want to come back quickly to the duty to collaborate. My anxiety with this is that, across the public sector, service leaders are apprised of the Prime Minister’s commitment to this issue. It was his first statement on the steps of Downing Street. Secretary of State Angela Rayner is behind it, leading the interministerial group. There is clarity across the public sector about what we want to achieve in dealing with the homelessness and rough sleeping problem in all the different areas of Government, whether we are talking about care leavers, prison release or in your area, Minister. That commitment is there today.

What I would like to understand is whether, in your view, the duty to collaborate that is being introduced through the Social Housing Bill is sufficient to outlast this Government? Is it enough? Is it going to achieve the culture change that we want to see so that, when we have all moved on and we are sipping our piña coladas in Northwich town centre at the piña colada festival, it will be sufficient to ensure that it will remain a priority in the NHS?

Alison McGovern: Let me say two things in response to that very reasonable question. The first one is just to reflect again on what has come up a number of times, which is that leadership matters. It is our duty as politicians to keep re-emphasising to NHS leaders that this is an important priority for us. There is no way to tackle homelessness and rough sleeping, or to get kids out of temporary accommodation, without leadership.

Neither you nor I could ever bind a future Parliament—we know this; elections do matter—but, on the very specific thing about the duty to collaborate, it is worth reflecting that one of the most important bits of homelessness legislation was passed in a private Member’s Bill by a Member of Parliament who is now a member of the Opposition and of the Conservative party. My experience as Minister of State for Homelessness was that leadership on this came from all sides of the House, and rightly so.

The duty to collaborate is a reflection on what might need to be improved in the duty to refer. In and of itself, legislation is never enough. I would welcome the Committee’s contribution in terms of where you think we can go further on accountability or culture change to try to impress upon people the importance of this issue. It takes leadership from the top, and then collaboration in local places. We would welcome the feedback of the Committee, given what you have heard, on where you think we need to go further.

Chair: I am very happy for our colleague from the HCLG Committee to have the last word. Thank you very much, Minister, for coming to this Committee today. We will look forward with eagerness to the correspondence that is promised, and I can assure you that we will keep at this in our various ways over the coming years.
